module.title: Unit 4: In the City: Places in Town & There is / There are
module.objective: Talk about places in town, give directions, and go shopping using 'there is / there are' and imperative verbs.

subModules.title: Reading Mission: Exploring Places in Town

content.summary: Welcome to your Reading Mission! In this module, you will read a short, fun passage about a small town and the places you can find there. You will practise understanding sentences with 'there is' and 'there are', learn vocabulary for places like parks, museums, and shops, and follow simple directions using imperative verbs like 'turn' and 'go'. By the end, you will feel confident reading about any town or city! Let's explore together!

linguisticTarget.grammar: There is + singular noun / There are + plural noun; some (positive) vs. any (negative & questions); imperative verbs for giving directions (Turn left. Go straight. Don't cross the road.)
linguisticTarget.vocabulary: Places in town (park, museum, library, supermarket, bank, hospital, chemist's, post office, train station, restaurant, café, cinema, bridge, square)
linguisticTarget.readingStrategy: Skim the passage first to understand the main idea (What is this text about?). Then scan for key details like place names, numbers, and direction words.

learningObjectives: Understand the main idea of a short A1 passage about places in a town.
Identify key details including specific places, their locations, and what you can do there.
Recognize and understand 'there is / there are' patterns with 'some' and 'any' in context.
Follow simple written directions using imperative verbs and prepositions of place.
Build confidence reading short descriptive texts about everyday environments.

contextWarmup.prompt: You are new in a town. You want to buy some bread. Where do you go?
contextWarmup.explanation: Great! You go to a supermarket to buy bread and other food. A library is for books, and a museum is for art or history. Knowing the right place for each activity is very useful when reading about towns!

rules: Use 'there is' (or 'there's') before a singular noun: 'There is a bank next to the post office.'
Use 'there are' before a plural noun: 'There are two restaurants in the square.'
Use 'some' in positive sentences: 'There are some shops on this street.' Use 'any' in negatives and questions: 'There aren't any cinemas here.' / 'Are there any parks?'
Imperative sentences use the base form of the verb without a subject: 'Turn right.' 'Go straight.' 'Don't cross the bridge.'
Prepositions of place help you describe where things are: behind, between, in front of, next to, opposite. Example: 'The café is between the bank and the library.'

commonTrap.explanation: Many beginners use 'there is' with plural nouns or forget to change 'some' to 'any' in negative sentences and questions. When you read, pay close attention to whether the noun after 'there is/are' is singular or plural, and check if the sentence is positive, negative, or a question.
commonTrap.wrong: There is many shops in the town. / There aren't some parks here.
commonTrap.correct: There are many shops in the town. / There aren't any parks here.

sections.title: Reading Passage: A Walk Around Greenfield

content.context: Emma is a new student in a small town called Greenfield. She writes an email to her friend about the town.
content.text:
Hi Mia!

I am in my new town. It is called Greenfield. It is small but very nice!

There is a big park in the centre of town. There are some beautiful trees and a small lake. Next to the park, there is a library. I go there every Saturday to read books.

There are some shops on Main Street. There is a supermarket, a chemist's, and a post office. The supermarket is between the chemist's and a café. There isn't a cinema, but there is a small museum opposite the library. It is free!

To get to my school from the park, you go straight on Park Road. Then turn left at the bridge. The school is next to the train station. Don't turn right — that road goes to the river!

There aren't any big restaurants here, but there are some nice cafés. I like the café in the square. It is in front of the museum.

I love Greenfield! Come and visit me!

Emma

highlights.note: 'There is' + singular noun (a big park) — used to say something exists.
'There are' + plural noun with 'some' — used in a positive sentence.
'There isn't' — negative form of 'there is' for singular nouns.
'There aren't any' — negative form of 'there are' with 'any' (not 'some').
'Opposite' means on the other side, facing the library.

highlights.text: between the chemist's and a café
highlights.note: 'Between' means in the middle of two things.
Imperative verb — a command or direction without a subject.
Negative imperative — 'Don't' + base verb to say 'do not do this'.

gistQuestion.prompt: What is the main idea of Emma's email?
options: Emma describes her new town and the places in it.
Emma asks Mia to help her find a cinema.
Emma is unhappy because her town is too small.
gistQuestion.explanation: Well done! Emma's email is about describing the places in her new town, Greenfield. She talks about the park, shops, museum, and how to get to her school. She is happy there!

detailQuestions.prompt: What is next to the park in Greenfield?
detailQuestions.explanation: The passage says: 'Next to the park, there is a library.' So the library is next to the park.

options: Between the chemist's and a café
detailQuestions.explanation: Emma writes: 'The supermarket is between the chemist's and a café.' The preposition 'between' tells us the supermarket is in the middle of these two places.

detailQuestions.prompt: How do you get to Emma's school from the park?
options: Go straight on Park Road, then turn left at the bridge.
Turn right at the bridge and go to the river.
Go to the museum and turn right.
detailQuestions.explanation: Emma gives clear directions: 'Go straight on Park Road. Then turn left at the bridge.' She also warns: 'Don't turn right — that road goes to the river!'

detailQuestions.prompt: Is there a cinema in Greenfield?
options: Yes, there is a big cinema.
Yes, it is opposite the library.
detailQuestions.explanation: The passage clearly states: 'There isn't a cinema.' This uses the negative form 'there isn't' to tell us the cinema does not exist in Greenfield.

questions.question: According to the passage, what is in the centre of Greenfield?
questions.explanation: Emma writes: 'There is a big park in the centre of town.' The park is the main place in the centre of Greenfield.

questions.question: Which sentence is correct based on the passage?
options: There are some shops on Main Street.
There are some shops on Park Road.
There aren't any shops in Greenfield.
questions.answer: There are some shops on Main Street.
questions.explanation: The passage says: 'There are some shops on Main Street.' Notice the use of 'some' in a positive sentence with the plural noun 'shops'.

questions.question: Where is the museum?
questions.explanation: Emma tells us: 'There is a small museum opposite the library.' The preposition 'opposite' means on the other side, facing the library.

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence about restaurants in Greenfield:
questions.explanation: In negative sentences with plural nouns, we use 'there aren't any' — not 'some'. The passage says: 'There aren't any big restaurants here.' This is the correct pattern.

questions.question: What does 'Don't turn right' mean in the passage?
options: It is a warning — do not go right because that road goes to the river.
It is a suggestion to turn right to find the school.
It means you must always turn right.
questions.answer: It is a warning — do not go right because that road goes to the river.
questions.explanation: 'Don't turn right' is a negative imperative. It tells you NOT to do something. Emma explains that turning right takes you to the river, not to the school.

questions.question: Where is the café that Emma likes?
options: In the square, in front of the museum
On Main Street, next to the supermarket
questions.answer: In the square, in front of the museum
questions.explanation: Emma writes: 'I like the café in the square. It is in front of the museum.' The preposition 'in front of' tells us the café faces the museum.

questions.question: Fill in the blank with the correct words: '_______ a small lake in the park.'
questions.explanation: 'Lake' is a singular noun, so we use 'There is'. The passage says: 'There are some beautiful trees and a small lake.' The lake is one item, so 'there is' is correct when we talk about it alone.

questions.question: Emma's school is next to which place?
questions.explanation: The passage states: 'The school is next to the train station.' The preposition 'next to' means very close, beside something.

subModules.title: Listening Mission: Getting Around the City

content.summary: In this listening mission, you will hear a conversation at a train station ticket office and a bookshop. You will practise understanding prices, directions, and descriptions of places in a city. Listen for key phrases like 'there is' and 'there are' to describe what you can find in a town. Pay attention to numbers and prices, because speakers often say them quickly. Also listen for polite requests like 'Can I help you?' and 'A ticket to London, please.' Focus on the speaker's tone to understand if they are asking a question or giving information.
learningObjectives: Understand spoken prices and amounts of money in British pounds
Recognise 'there is' and 'there are' when speakers describe places in a city
Identify polite requests and offers of help in shops and ticket offices
Understand simple directions and descriptions of places in town

keyPhrases.note: A polite question used by shop assistants and staff to offer help to a customer.
A polite way to ask for a ticket. Use 'a ticket to + place + please' to buy travel tickets.

keyPhrases.phrase: There is a bookshop near the station.
keyPhrases.meaning: Ada sebuah toko buku dekat stasiun.
keyPhrases.note: Use 'there is' with singular nouns to say something exists in a place.

keyPhrases.phrase: There are two cafes on this street.
keyPhrases.meaning: Ada dua kafe di jalan ini.
keyPhrases.note: Use 'there are' with plural nouns to say multiple things exist in a place.
A common phrase when you give something to someone, like money or a ticket.
A basic question to ask the price of something in a shop or ticket office.

connectedSpeech.note: In fast speech, 'Can I' blends together so 'can' loses its full vowel and becomes a weak /kən/. The two words sound like one: 'k'nai'. The 'you' at the end also weakens to /jə/.
In natural speech, 'you are' contracts and blends into one syllable: 'y'are' sounds like /jɑːr/. The phrase sounds like two beats: 'HERE-yar'.
'There is' almost always contracts to 'there's' in spoken English. The /ɪz/ reduces to just /z/ attached to 'there'. This is very common and natural at all levels.
In fast speech, 'it is' contracts to 'it's'. The word 'pounds' is often dropped when the context is clear. Also, 'seven' may lose the final /n/ and become /sɛvm/ before 'fifty'.

sections.title: Audio Dialogue: At the Train Station and the Bookshop

content.context: Sarah is visiting a new city for the day. First, she goes to the train station ticket office to buy a ticket to London. The ticket seller, Tom, helps her. After buying the ticket, Sarah asks about places near the station and finds a bookshop nearby.
content.audioPrompt: Listen carefully to the following dialogue between Sarah and Tom at a train station ticket office, and then Sarah exploring the area nearby.

lines.speaker: Sarah
lines.text: Yes, please. A ticket to London, please. Return.
lines.translation: Ya, tolong. Satu tiket ke London. Pulang pergi.

lines.speaker: Tom
lines.text: OK, a day return. Well, it's twenty-seven pounds fifty, but you can't come back between four o'clock and seven o'clock.
lines.translation: Oke, tiket pulang pergi satu hari. Nah, harganya dua puluh tujuh pound lima puluh, tapi Anda tidak bisa pulang antara jam empat dan jam tujuh.

lines.speaker: Sarah
lines.text: Oh, no problem. Here you are - thirty pounds.
lines.translation: Oh, tidak masalah. Ini dia - tiga puluh pound.

lines.speaker: Tom
lines.text: Thank you. And two pounds fifty change. Have a nice trip!
lines.translation: Terima kasih. Dan kembalian dua pound lima puluh. Semoga perjalanan menyenangkan!

lines.speaker: Sarah
lines.text: Thanks! Excuse me, is there a bookshop near the station?
lines.translation: Terima kasih! Permisi, apakah ada toko buku dekat stasiun?

lines.speaker: Tom
lines.text: Yes, there is. Go straight and turn left. There is a bookshop next to the cafe.
lines.translation: Ya, ada. Jalan lurus dan belok kiri. Ada toko buku di sebelah kafe.

lines.speaker: Sarah
lines.text: Great! Are there any restaurants near there too?
lines.translation: Bagus! Apakah ada restoran di dekat situ juga?

lines.speaker: Tom
lines.text: Yes, there are two restaurants on Park Street. They are very good!
lines.translation: Ya, ada dua restoran di Park Street. Mereka sangat bagus!

lines.speaker: Sarah
lines.text: Wonderful, thank you so much! I have my ticket and now I know where to go. See you later!
lines.translation: Luar biasa, terima kasih banyak! Saya sudah punya tiket dan sekarang saya tahu harus ke mana. Sampai jumpa!

subModules.title: Writing Mission: Describing Your City & Giving Directions

content.summary: In this writing lesson, you will learn how to write sentences and short paragraphs about places in a city. You will use 'there is' with one thing (singular) and 'there are' with more than one thing (plural). You will also learn to write directions using imperative verbs like 'turn', 'go', and 'walk'. Finally, you will use prepositions of place such as 'next to', 'opposite', and 'between' to describe where places are located.

blueprintItems.title: Describe One Place with 'There is'
blueprintItems.formula: There is + a/an + singular noun + location phrase.
blueprintItems.example: There is a hospital next to the park.

blueprintItems.title: Describe Many Places with 'There are'
blueprintItems.formula: There are + number/some + plural noun + location phrase.
blueprintItems.example: There are three restaurants in front of the museum.

blueprintItems.title: Use 'some' and 'any' Correctly
blueprintItems.formula: Positive: There are some + plural noun. Negative: There aren't any + plural noun. Question: Are there any + plural noun?
blueprintItems.example: There are some shops on Main Street. There aren't any banks near my house. Are there any supermarkets in your town?

blueprintItems.title: Give Directions with Imperative Verbs
blueprintItems.example: Turn left at the traffic light. Go straight for two blocks. Walk past the library.

blueprintItems.title: Describe Locations with Prepositions of Place
blueprintItems.formula: The + place + is + preposition of place + the + other place.
blueprintItems.example: The bank is opposite the library. The café is between the bookshop and the pharmacy.

mechanicsRules.rule: Always capitalize the first word of a sentence and proper nouns (names of specific places, streets, or cities).
mechanicsRules.badExample: there is a park on green street.
mechanicsRules.goodExample: There is a park on Green Street.
mechanicsRules.why: Sentences must start with a capital letter. Street names and city names are proper nouns, so they always need capital letters.

mechanicsRules.rule: Use a period (.) at the end of a statement. Use a question mark (?) at the end of a question.
mechanicsRules.badExample: Are there any shops near here.
mechanicsRules.goodExample: Are there any shops near here?
mechanicsRules.why: Questions must end with a question mark so the reader knows it is a question, not a statement.

mechanicsRules.rule: Use 'a' before consonant sounds and 'an' before vowel sounds when introducing a singular place for the first time.
mechanicsRules.badExample: There is a airport in the city.
mechanicsRules.goodExample: There is an airport in the city.
mechanicsRules.why: The word 'airport' starts with a vowel sound ('a'), so we use 'an' instead of 'a'. This makes the sentence easier to read and say.

mechanicsRules.rule: Do not add 's' to the noun after 'There is'. Do not forget 's' on the noun after 'There are'.
mechanicsRules.badExample: There is two parks. There are a shop.
mechanicsRules.goodExample: There are two parks. There is a shop.
mechanicsRules.why: 'There is' goes with one thing (singular). 'There are' goes with more than one thing (plural). Match the verb to the noun.

guidedLabChallenges.title: Challenge 1: Describe Your Town
guidedLabChallenges.instruction: Write a short paragraph (at least 4 sentences) describing your town or city. Use 'there is' for one place and 'there are' for more than one place. practicumQuestions.prompt: Write a short paragraph (at least 5 sentences) about a city you like or want to visit. Describe what places are there using 'there is', 'there are', 'some', and 'any'. Use at least two different prepositions of place.
practicumQuestions.criteria: The answer must contain at least 5 complete sentences. The paragraph uses 'there is' and 'there are' correctly. 'Some' is used in at least one positive sentence. 'Any' is used in a negative sentence or a question. At least two different prepositions of place are included. Proper nouns are capitalized. All sentences end with correct punctuation.
practicumQuestions.sampleGoodAnswer: I want to visit Jakarta. There are some tall buildings in the city centre. There is a big museum called the National Museum. There are many restaurants behind the shopping mall. There is a beautiful park next to the river. There aren't any mountains in Jakarta, but there are some beaches near the city.

subModules.title: Speaking Lab: Talking About Places in Town & Giving Directions

content.summary: In this speaking lab, you will practise talking about places in a city or town, giving simple directions, and describing what is in your neighbourhood using 'there is' and 'there are'. You will learn how to pronounce place names clearly, use rising intonation for yes/no questions like 'Is there a bank?', and use falling intonation for statements like 'There is a park next to the school.' You will also practise imperative verbs for directions such as 'turn left', 'go straight', and 'cross the street'.
content.audioGuidance: Pay attention to the /ð/ sound in 'there' — put your tongue gently between your teeth and let air flow out. For the word 'street', make sure you pronounce the consonant cluster /str/ clearly without adding an extra vowel before it. When you say 'Turn right', stress the word 'right' to make your direction clear. In yes/no questions like 'Is there a hospital?', let your voice go UP at the end. In statements like 'There is a library on Main Street', let your voice go DOWN at the end.

pillars.name: Place Vocabulary Clarity
pillars.target: Clear pronunciation of city place names
pillars.explanation: Practise saying place words like 'supermarket', 'library', 'hospital', 'restaurant', and 'pharmacy' with correct syllable stress. For example, say 'SU-per-mar-ket' with stress on the first syllable, and 'res-TAU-rant' with stress on the second syllable. Clear pronunciation helps people understand which place you are talking about.

pillars.name: There is / There are Delivery
pillars.target: Smooth and natural use of existential structures
pillars.explanation: When you speak, connect 'there is' smoothly so it sounds like 'there-iz' and 'there are' like 'there-ar'. Do not pause between the two words. In negative forms, say 'there ISN'T' and 'there AREN'T' with a clear stress on the negative contraction. This makes your speech sound natural and easy to understand.

pillars.name: Direction-Giving Intonation
pillars.target: Confident imperative tone for giving directions
pillars.explanation: When giving directions, use a clear and steady voice. Imperative sentences like 'Turn left at the bank' and 'Go straight ahead' should have a gentle falling intonation at the end. Stress the key direction words: 'TURN LEFT', 'GO STRAIGHT', 'CROSS the street'. This helps the listener follow your instructions easily.

pillars.name: Question Intonation for Location
pillars.target: Correct rising intonation in yes/no location questions
pillars.explanation: When you ask 'Is there a park near here?' or 'Are there any shops on this street?', your voice should rise at the end of the sentence. This rising pattern tells the listener that you are asking a question and you expect a 'yes' or 'no' answer. Practise the upward pitch movement on the last word.

stressPairs.shiftExplanation: In 'LIBRARY', the stress is on the first syllable 'LI'. When it becomes 'LIBRARIAN' (a person who works in a library), the stress shifts to the second syllable 'BRA'. Notice how the emphasis moves forward in the longer word.

In 'SUPERMARKET', the main stress is on the first syllable 'SU'. When we add 'SHOPPER' to make a compound phrase, the primary stress shifts to 'SHOP'. This is common in English compound noun phrases where the second word carries the main stress.

In 'OPPOSITE', the stress is on the first syllable 'OP'. When the word changes to 'OPPOSITION', the stress shifts to the third syllable 'SI'. Words ending in '-tion' often pull the stress to the syllable just before the suffix.

drills.targetText: There is a hospital on Park Street.
drills.phonetic: /ðɛr ɪz ə ˈhɒs.pɪ.təl ɒn pɑːk striːt/
drills.focus: Smooth 'there is' linking and clear /ð/ sound
drills.hint: Place your tongue between your teeth for the 'th' in 'there'. Link 'there' and 'is' together smoothly: 'there-iz'. Stress 'HOS-pi-tal' on the first syllable.

drills.targetText: There are two banks next to the post office.
drills.phonetic: /ðɛr ɑːr tuː bæŋks nɛkst tə ðə pəʊst ˈɒf.ɪs/
drills.hint: Say 'there are' smoothly as 'there-ar'. Make sure you clearly say the /ks/ sound at the end of 'banks' and 'next'. Stress 'POST' in 'post office'.

drills.targetText: Turn left at the traffic lights and go straight ahead.
drills.phonetic: /tɜːn lɛft æt ðə ˈtræf.ɪk laɪts ænd ɡəʊ streɪt əˈhɛd/
drills.hint: Stress the direction words: 'TURN LEFT' and 'GO STRAIGHT'. Say 'straight' with a clear /str/ cluster — do not add a vowel before it. Let your voice fall at the end of the instruction.

drills.targetText: Is there a pharmacy near here?
drills.hint: This is a yes/no question, so your voice should go UP on the last word 'here'. Stress the second syllable of 'phar-MA-cy'. Keep the question short and clear.

drills.targetText: The restaurant is between the bank and the bookshop.
drills.phonetic: /ðə ˈrɛs.tə.rɒnt ɪz bɪˈtwiːn ðə bæŋk ænd ðə ˈbʊk.ʃɒp/
drills.focus: Preposition of place 'between' and place vocabulary
drills.hint: Stress 'RES-tau-rant' on the first syllable. Say 'between' with stress on the second syllable: 'be-TWEEN'. Make sure you pronounce the /ʃ/ sound in 'bookshop' clearly.

drills.targetText: Cross the road and the museum is on your left.
drills.phonetic: /krɒs ðə rəʊd ænd ðə mjuːˈziː.əm ɪz ɒn jɔːr lɛft/
drills.hint: Start with a strong, clear 'CROSS'. Say 'museum' with stress on the second syllable: 'mu-ZE-um'. Use falling intonation at the end because this is a statement giving directions.

roleplay.context: You are visiting a new city and you stop to ask Mr. Khoirul for directions. He is standing near a map of the town centre. You want to find the supermarket, ask about nearby places, and describe what is in your own town. Practise using 'there is', 'there are', prepositions of place, and imperative direction verbs.

turns.speaker: Mr. Khoirul
turns.text: Hello! Let's practice giving directions. Imagine you're at the restaurant on the map. Can you tell me how to get to the supermarket?
turns.translation: Halo! Ayo berlatih memberikan petunjuk arah. Bayangkan kamu ada di restoran di peta. Bisakah kamu memberi tahu saya cara ke supermarket?

turns.speaker: You
turns.text: OK, turn right and go down King Street. The supermarket is on the right.
turns.translation: Oke, belok kanan dan jalan terus di King Street. Supermarketnya ada di sebelah kanan.

turns.speaker: Mr. Khoirul
turns.text: Perfect! That's very clear. Now, can you tell me: are there any parks near the supermarket?
turns.translation: Sempurna! Itu sangat jelas. Sekarang, bisakah kamu memberi tahu saya: apakah ada taman di dekat supermarket?

turns.speaker: You
turns.text: Yes, there is. There is a park next to the supermarket on Green Street.
turns.translation: Ya, ada. Ada sebuah taman di sebelah supermarket di Green Street.

turns.speaker: Mr. Khoirul
turns.text: Excellent! You're doing great. One more question: Is there a library in your town? Where is it?
turns.translation: Luar biasa! Kamu hebat. Satu pertanyaan lagi: Apakah ada perpustakaan di kotamu? Di mana letaknya?

turns.speaker: You
turns.text: Yes, there is. The library is opposite the restaurant, behind the bank.
turns.translation: Ya, ada. Perpustakaannya ada di seberang restoran, di belakang bank.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Tell a short story about your town. Describe the places in your town and where they are located. Use 'there is' and 'there are' and prepositions of place. Follow the three story points below to guide your story.
practicumQuestions.audioPrompt: Now it's your turn to tell me about your town! Describe the places you can find there. Where are they? What is near what? Tell me a short story using 'there is' and 'there are'.
storyPoints: Start by saying the name of your town and mention two or three important places (for example: a school, a hospital, a park).
Describe where these places are using prepositions like 'next to', 'opposite', 'between', or 'behind'.
End by saying what your favourite place is and why you like it (for example: 'My favourite place is the park because it is big and beautiful').
practicumQuestions.targetSentence: I live in a small town. There is a school next to the hospital. There are two parks near my house. My favourite place is the park because it is big and beautiful.
practicumQuestions.phonetic: /aɪ lɪv ɪn ə smɔːl taʊn. ðɛr ɪz ə skuːl nɛkst tə ðə ˈhɒs.pɪ.təl. ðɛr ɑːr tuː pɑːks nɪər maɪ haʊs. maɪ ˈfeɪ.vər.ɪt pleɪs ɪz ðə pɑːk bɪˈkɒz ɪt ɪz bɪɡ ænd ˈbjuː.tɪ.fəl/
practicumQuestions.hint: Remember to use 'there is' for one thing and 'there are' for two or more things. Use prepositions like 'next to', 'near', 'opposite' to describe locations.
practicumQuestions.explanation: This storytelling task helps you practise describing places in your town using existential structures ('there is/are') and prepositions of place. Speaking in connected sentences builds your fluency and confidence at A1 level.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Tell a short story about walking through a city centre. Describe what you see and the directions you take. Use imperative verbs like 'turn', 'go', and 'cross', and describe places using 'there is' and 'there are'.
practicumQuestions.audioPrompt: Imagine you are walking through a city centre. Tell me what you see and how you walk from one place to another. Use direction words and describe the places around you!
storyPoints: Start at a specific place (for example: 'I start at the train station') and describe what is near it.
Give directions to walk to another place (for example: 'I turn left and go straight. There is a big supermarket on the right').
Arrive at your final destination and describe what is around it (for example: 'I arrive at the museum. There are beautiful gardens opposite the museum').
practicumQuestions.targetSentence: I start at the train station. There is a café next to the station. I turn left and go straight down Main Street. There is a big supermarket on the right. I cross the road and arrive at the museum. There are beautiful gardens opposite the museum.
practicumQuestions.phonetic: /aɪ stɑːt æt ðə treɪn ˈsteɪ.ʃən. ðɛr ɪz ə ˈkæf.eɪ nɛkst tə ðə ˈsteɪ.ʃən. aɪ tɜːn lɛft ænd ɡəʊ streɪt daʊn meɪn striːt. ðɛr ɪz ə bɪɡ ˈsuː.pə.mɑː.kɪt ɒn ðə raɪt. aɪ krɒs ðə rəʊd ænd əˈraɪv æt ðə mjuːˈziː.əm. ðɛr ɑːr ˈbjuː.tɪ.fəl ˈɡɑː.dənz ˈɒp.ə.zɪt ðə mjuːˈziː.əm/
practicumQuestions.hint: Use imperative verbs at the start of direction sentences: 'Turn left', 'Go straight', 'Cross the road'. Then describe what you see with 'there is' or 'there are'.
practicumQuestions.explanation: This storytelling task combines direction-giving with place descriptions. Practising both skills together helps you speak more naturally when navigating or describing a city, which is a key real-world A1 speaking skill.

practicumQuestions.instruction: You are a tourist in a new city. You are lost and you call Mr. Khoirul, a local guide, to ask for directions to the nearest hospital. Use polite questions with 'Is there...?' and listen to his directions.
practicumQuestions.audioPrompt: Ring ring! Hello, this is Mr. Khoirul, your local city guide. How can I help you today?
practicumQuestions.scenarioContext: You are a tourist visiting a new city for the first time. You feel unwell and need to find the nearest hospital. You call Mr. Khoirul, a friendly local guide, to ask where the hospital is and how to get there from the main square.
practicumQuestions.characterRole: Mr. Khoirul is a friendly and patient local city guide who knows every street and building in the city. He speaks slowly and clearly to help tourists find their way.
practicumQuestions.targetSentence: Excuse me, is there a hospital near here? How do I get there from the main square?
practicumQuestions.phonetic: /ɪkˈskjuːz miː, ɪz ðɛr ə ˈhɒs.pɪ.təl nɪər hɪər? haʊ duː aɪ ɡɛt ðɛr frɒm ðə meɪn skwɛər/
practicumQuestions.hint: Start politely with 'Excuse me'. Use 'Is there a...?' to ask about a place. Ask 'How do I get there?' to request directions.
practicumQuestions.explanation: This roleplay practises asking for locations and directions in a real-life emergency-like situation. Using 'Is there...?' questions and polite openers is essential for A1 communication in a city.

practicumQuestions.instruction: You are at a tourist information centre. Mr. Khoirul works there. Ask him about places to visit in the city. Use 'Are there any...?' questions and describe what kind of places you want to see.
practicumQuestions.audioPrompt: Welcome to the City Tourist Information Centre! I'm Mr. Khoirul. What kind of places would you like to visit today?
practicumQuestions.scenarioContext: You have just arrived in a new city and you go to the tourist information centre to learn about interesting places to visit. You want to know about museums, parks, and restaurants in the city centre.
practicumQuestions.characterRole: Mr. Khoirul is a helpful tourist information officer. He has maps and brochures and loves to recommend places to visitors. He answers questions clearly and gives simple directions.
practicumQuestions.targetSentence: Are there any museums in the city centre? I also want to visit a park. Is there a good restaurant near the museum?
practicumQuestions.phonetic: /ɑːr ðɛr ˈɛn.i mjuːˈziː.əmz ɪn ðə ˈsɪt.i ˈsɛn.tər? aɪ ˈɔːl.səʊ wɒnt tə ˈvɪz.ɪt ə pɑːk. ɪz ðɛr ə ɡʊd ˈrɛs.tə.rɒnt nɪər ðə mjuːˈziː.əm/
practicumQuestions.hint: Use 'Are there any...?' for plural questions and 'Is there a...?' for singular questions. Say what you want to do: 'I want to visit...'
practicumQuestions.explanation: This roleplay builds confidence in asking about multiple places using both singular and plural forms of 'there is/are'. Interacting at a tourist centre is a very common A1 real-world scenario.

practicumQuestions.instruction: You are helping Mr. Khoirul, a new visitor, find his way around your town. He calls you on the phone and asks for directions from the train station to the library. Give him clear step-by-step directions.
practicumQuestions.audioPrompt: Hello! This is Mr. Khoirul. I just arrived at the train station and I need to go to the library. Can you help me? How do I get there?
practicumQuestions.scenarioContext: Mr. Khoirul is visiting your town for the first time. He is at the train station and needs to walk to the library. You know the town very well and you need to give him clear, simple directions using imperative verbs and prepositions of place.
practicumQuestions.characterRole: Mr. Khoirul is a polite visitor who does not know the town at all. He asks simple questions and needs step-by-step directions. He may ask you to repeat or clarify.
practicumQuestions.targetSentence: Go out of the train station and turn right. Go straight down Oak Street. The library is on the left, next to the post office.
practicumQuestions.phonetic: /ɡəʊ aʊt ɒv ðə treɪn ˈsteɪ.ʃən ænd tɜːn raɪt. ɡəʊ streɪt daʊn əʊk striːt. ðə ˈlaɪ.brər.i ɪz ɒn ðə lɛft, nɛkst tə ðə pəʊst ˈɒf.ɪs/
practicumQuestions.hint: Use imperative verbs to start each direction: 'Go...', 'Turn...', 'Walk...'. Then describe the final location with 'on the left/right' or 'next to'.
practicumQuestions.explanation: This roleplay reverses the usual role — you are the direction-giver. Practising giving clear step-by-step directions using imperatives and prepositions is a core A1 speaking skill for real-life navigation.

practicumQuestions.instruction: You are at a small shop in the city. Mr. Khoirul is the shopkeeper. Ask him about products in the shop using 'Is there...?' and 'Are there...?' and buy something you need.
practicumQuestions.audioPrompt: Good morning! Welcome to my shop. I'm Mr. Khoirul. We have many things here. What are you looking for today?
practicumQuestions.scenarioContext: You are shopping in a small city shop. You need to buy a map of the city and some water. You also want to know if the shop sells postcards. Mr. Khoirul is the friendly shopkeeper who can help you find what you need.
practicumQuestions.characterRole: Mr. Khoirul is a cheerful shopkeeper in a small city shop. He sells maps, postcards, drinks, snacks, and souvenirs. He is happy to help customers and answers their questions with a smile.
practicumQuestions.targetSentence: Good morning! Is there a city map? I need one, please. Are there any postcards? And I would like a bottle of water, please.
practicumQuestions.phonetic: /ɡʊd ˈmɔː.nɪŋ! ɪz ðɛr ə ˈsɪt.i mæp? aɪ niːd wʌn pliːz. ɑːr ðɛr ˈɛn.i ˈpəʊst.kɑːdz? ænd aɪ wʊd laɪk ə ˈbɒt.əl ɒv ˈwɔː.tər pliːz/
practicumQuestions.hint: Use 'Is there a...?' for one item and 'Are there any...?' for items that might be plural. Always say 'please' to be polite when buying things.
practicumQuestions.explanation: This roleplay practises using 'there is/are' in a shopping context, which is a practical A1 skill. Combining location language with transactional language prepares you for real interactions in shops.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Say the following sentence out loud. Focus on pronouncing each place name clearly and correctly.
practicumQuestions.audioPrompt: Please say this sentence clearly. Pay attention to the place vocabulary words.
practicumQuestions.targetSentence: There is a pharmacy between the supermarket and the library.
practicumQuestions.phonetic: /ðɛr ɪz ə ˈfɑː.mə.si bɪˈtwiːn ðə ˈsuː.pə.mɑː.kɪt ænd ðə ˈlaɪ.brər.i/
practicumQuestions.hint: Say 'PHAR-ma-cy' with stress on the first syllable. 'SU-per-mar-ket' also has stress on the first syllable. 'LI-bra-ry' has stress on the first syllable — do not skip the middle syllable 'bra'.
practicumQuestions.explanation: This drill tests your ability to clearly pronounce key city place vocabulary. At A1 level, being able to say place names correctly is essential for asking and giving directions in a town.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Say the following sentence out loud. Focus on using the correct form: 'there is' for singular and 'there are' for plural.
practicumQuestions.audioPrompt: Please say this sentence. Be careful with 'there is' and 'there are' — one is for singular, the other is for plural.
practicumQuestions.targetSentence: There is one hospital in my town, but there are three schools and two parks.
practicumQuestions.phonetic: /ðɛr ɪz wʌn ˈhɒs.pɪ.təl ɪn maɪ taʊn, bʌt ðɛr ɑːr θriː skuːlz ænd tuː pɑːks/
practicumQuestions.hint: Use 'there IS' before 'one hospital' (singular). Use 'there ARE' before 'three schools' and 'two parks' (plural). Link 'there is' and 'there are' smoothly without long pauses.
practicumQuestions.explanation: This grammar drill reinforces the singular/plural distinction between 'there is' and 'there are'. Correct subject-verb agreement in existential sentences is a fundamental A1 grammar point that directly affects how natural your spoken English sounds.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Say both words out loud and notice how the syllable stress shifts. First say 'OPPOSITE', then say 'OPPOSITION'. Exaggerate the stressed syllable.
practicumQuestions.audioPrompt: Listen carefully to the stress change. Say 'OPPOSITE' — stress on 'OP'. Now say 'OPPOSITION' — stress on 'SI'. Say both words clearly.
practicumQuestions.targetSentence: The bank is OPPOSITE the park. There is strong OPPOSITION to the new road.
practicumQuestions.phonetic: /ðə bæŋk ɪz ˈɒp.ə.zɪt ðə pɑːk. ðɛr ɪz strɒŋ ˌɒp.əˈzɪʃ.ən tə ðə njuː rəʊd/
practicumQuestions.hint: In 'OPPOSITE', stress the first syllable: 'OP-po-site'. In 'OPPOSITION', the stress moves to the third syllable: 'op-po-SI-tion'. Clap on the stressed syllable to feel the rhythm change.
practicumQuestions.explanation: This drill practises syllable stress shift between related words. Understanding how stress moves when word forms change is important for clear pronunciation. At A1 level, 'opposite' is a key preposition for describing locations, so pronouncing it correctly is especially useful.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Say both sentences out loud. Use RISING intonation (voice goes up) for the yes/no question and FALLING intonation (voice goes down) for the statement. Feel the difference in your voice.
practicumQuestions.audioPrompt: Now practise intonation! For the question 'Is there a bank near here?', your voice goes UP at the end. For the statement 'There is a bank on Main Street', your voice goes DOWN at the end. Say both sentences now.
practicumQuestions.targetSentence: Is there a bank near here? ↗ There is a bank on Main Street. ↘
practicumQuestions.phonetic: /ɪz ðɛr ə bæŋk nɪər hɪər ↗ / /ðɛr ɪz ə bæŋk ɒn meɪn striːt ↘/
practicumQuestions.hint: For the question, imagine your voice is climbing stairs at the end — it goes UP on 'here?'. For the statement, imagine your voice is going down a slide — it goes DOWN on 'Street.' Practise the contrast several times.
practicumQuestions.explanation: This intonation drill practises the essential difference between rising intonation in yes/no questions and falling intonation in declarative statements. Mastering this pattern helps listeners understand whether you are asking a question or making a statement, which is critical for clear A1-level communication about places and directions.

reading.question: According to the passage, what is in the centre of Greenfield?
reading.explanation: Emma writes: 'There is a big park in the centre of town.' The park is the main place in the centre of Greenfield.

reading.question: Which sentence is correct based on the passage?
options: There are some shops on Main Street.
There are some shops on Park Road.
There aren't any shops in Greenfield.
reading.answer: There are some shops on Main Street.
reading.explanation: The passage says: 'There are some shops on Main Street.' Notice the use of 'some' in a positive sentence with the plural noun 'shops'.

reading.question: Where is the museum?
reading.explanation: Emma tells us: 'There is a small museum opposite the library.' The preposition 'opposite' means on the other side, facing the library.

reading.question: Choose the correct sentence about restaurants in Greenfield:
reading.explanation: In negative sentences with plural nouns, we use 'there aren't any' — not 'some'. The passage says: 'There aren't any big restaurants here.' This is the correct pattern.

reading.question: What does 'Don't turn right' mean in the passage?
options: It is a warning — do not go right because that road goes to the river.
It is a suggestion to turn right to find the school.
It means you must always turn right.
reading.answer: It is a warning — do not go right because that road goes to the river.
reading.explanation: 'Don't turn right' is a negative imperative. It tells you NOT to do something. Emma explains that turning right takes you to the river, not to the school.

reading.question: Where is the café that Emma likes?
options: In the square, in front of the museum
On Main Street, next to the supermarket
reading.answer: In the square, in front of the museum
reading.explanation: Emma writes: 'I like the café in the square. It is in front of the museum.' The preposition 'in front of' tells us the café faces the museum.

reading.question: Fill in the blank with the correct words: '_______ a small lake in the park.'
reading.explanation: 'Lake' is a singular noun, so we use 'There is'. The passage says: 'There are some beautiful trees and a small lake.' The lake is one item, so 'there is' is correct when we talk about it alone.

reading.question: Emma's school is next to which place?
reading.explanation: The passage states: 'The school is next to the train station.' The preposition 'next to' means very close, beside something.

reading.question: What is the weather like when it is raining?
reading.explanation: Rain brings water, making the weather and ground wet.

reading.question: Choose the correct form: 'They _____ playing football right now.'
reading.explanation: 'They' requires the plural auxiliary 'are' in present continuous.

reading.question: What is Jamie's nationality?
reading.explanation: Jamie is from Spain, so his nationality is Spanish.

reading.question: Which sentence is the correct negative form of 'She likes coffee'?
reading.explanation: For third person singular (she/he/it), we use 'doesn't + base verb'.

reading.question: Where do they usually eat dinner on weekdays?
reading.explanation: Daily routines typically describe having dinner at home with family.

reading.question: What time does the train to London depart?
reading.explanation: Standard timetable questions provide specific morning departure times.

writing.prompt: Write 3 sentences about your neighbourhood. Use 'there is' in one sentence, 'there are' in another sentence, and a preposition of place (next to, opposite, behind, between, or in front of) in at least one sentence.
writing.criteria: The answer must contain at least 3 complete sentences. One sentence uses 'there is' with a singular noun. One sentence uses 'there are' with a plural noun. At least one preposition of place is used correctly. All sentences start with a capital letter and end with a period.
writing.sampleGoodAnswer: There is a small park near my house. There are two shops opposite the park. The school is between the mosque and the hospital.

writing.prompt: Your friend wants to visit a café in your town. Write directions from the bus stop to the café. Use at least 3 imperative sentences (for example: Turn left. Go straight. Walk past the bank.).
writing.criteria: The answer must contain at least 3 imperative sentences giving clear directions. Each sentence uses a base verb (turn, go, walk, cross, etc.) without a subject. Sentences are correctly capitalized and punctuated. The directions are logical and easy to follow.
writing.sampleGoodAnswer: Walk out of the bus stop and turn right. Go straight for one block. Walk past the bookshop and the bank. Turn left at the traffic light. The café is on your right, next to the pharmacy.

writing.prompt: Write a short paragraph (at least 5 sentences) about a city you like or want to visit. Describe what places are there using 'there is', 'there are', 'some', and 'any'. Use at least two different prepositions of place.
writing.criteria: The answer must contain at least 5 complete sentences. The paragraph uses 'there is' and 'there are' correctly. 'Some' is used in at least one positive sentence. 'Any' is used in a negative sentence or a question. At least two different prepositions of place are included. Proper nouns are capitalized. All sentences end with correct punctuation.
writing.sampleGoodAnswer: I want to visit Jakarta. There are some tall buildings in the city centre. There is a big museum called the National Museum. There are many restaurants behind the shopping mall. There is a beautiful park next to the river. There aren't any mountains in Jakarta, but there are some beaches near the city.

speaking.instruction: Tell a short story about your town. Describe the places in your town and where they are located. Use 'there is' and 'there are' and prepositions of place. Follow the three story points below to guide your story.
speaking.audioPrompt: Now it's your turn to tell me about your town! Describe the places you can find there. Where are they? What is near what? Tell me a short story using 'there is' and 'there are'.
storyPoints: Start by saying the name of your town and mention two or three important places (for example: a school, a hospital, a park).
Describe where these places are using prepositions like 'next to', 'opposite', 'between', or 'behind'.
End by saying what your favourite place is and why you like it (for example: 'My favourite place is the park because it is big and beautiful').
speaking.targetSentence: I live in a small town. There is a school next to the hospital. There are two parks near my house. My favourite place is the park because it is big and beautiful.
speaking.phonetic: /aɪ lɪv ɪn ə smɔːl taʊn. ðɛr ɪz ə skuːl nɛkst tə ðə ˈhɒs.pɪ.təl. ðɛr ɑːr tuː pɑːks nɪər maɪ haʊs. maɪ ˈfeɪ.vər.ɪt pleɪs ɪz ðə pɑːk bɪˈkɒz ɪt ɪz bɪɡ ænd ˈbjuː.tɪ.fəl/
speaking.hint: Remember to use 'there is' for one thing and 'there are' for two or more things. Use prepositions like 'next to', 'near', 'opposite' to describe locations.
speaking.explanation: This storytelling task helps you practise describing places in your town using existential structures ('there is/are') and prepositions of place. Speaking in connected sentences builds your fluency and confidence at A1 level.

speaking.instruction: Tell a short story about walking through a city centre. Describe what you see and the directions you take. Use imperative verbs like 'turn', 'go', and 'cross', and describe places using 'there is' and 'there are'.
speaking.audioPrompt: Imagine you are walking through a city centre. Tell me what you see and how you walk from one place to another. Use direction words and describe the places around you!
storyPoints: Start at a specific place (for example: 'I start at the train station') and describe what is near it.
Give directions to walk to another place (for example: 'I turn left and go straight. There is a big supermarket on the right').
Arrive at your final destination and describe what is around it (for example: 'I arrive at the museum. There are beautiful gardens opposite the museum').
speaking.targetSentence: I start at the train station. There is a café next to the station. I turn left and go straight down Main Street. There is a big supermarket on the right. I cross the road and arrive at the museum. There are beautiful gardens opposite the museum.
speaking.phonetic: /aɪ stɑːt æt ðə treɪn ˈsteɪ.ʃən. ðɛr ɪz ə ˈkæf.eɪ nɛkst tə ðə ˈsteɪ.ʃən. aɪ tɜːn lɛft ænd ɡəʊ streɪt daʊn meɪn striːt. ðɛr ɪz ə bɪɡ ˈsuː.pə.mɑː.kɪt ɒn ðə raɪt. aɪ krɒs ðə rəʊd ænd əˈraɪv æt ðə mjuːˈziː.əm. ðɛr ɑːr ˈbjuː.tɪ.fəl ˈɡɑː.dənz ˈɒp.ə.zɪt ðə mjuːˈziː.əm/
speaking.hint: Use imperative verbs at the start of direction sentences: 'Turn left', 'Go straight', 'Cross the road'. Then describe what you see with 'there is' or 'there are'.
speaking.explanation: This storytelling task combines direction-giving with place descriptions. Practising both skills together helps you speak more naturally when navigating or describing a city, which is a key real-world A1 speaking skill.

speaking.instruction: You are a tourist in a new city. You are lost and you call Mr. Khoirul, a local guide, to ask for directions to the nearest hospital. Use polite questions with 'Is there...?' and listen to his directions.
speaking.audioPrompt: Ring ring! Hello, this is Mr. Khoirul, your local city guide. How can I help you today?
speaking.scenarioContext: You are a tourist visiting a new city for the first time. You feel unwell and need to find the nearest hospital. You call Mr. Khoirul, a friendly local guide, to ask where the hospital is and how to get there from the main square.
speaking.characterRole: Mr. Khoirul is a friendly and patient local city guide who knows every street and building in the city. He speaks slowly and clearly to help tourists find their way.
speaking.targetSentence: Excuse me, is there a hospital near here? How do I get there from the main square?
speaking.phonetic: /ɪkˈskjuːz miː, ɪz ðɛr ə ˈhɒs.pɪ.təl nɪər hɪər? haʊ duː aɪ ɡɛt ðɛr frɒm ðə meɪn skwɛər/
speaking.hint: Start politely with 'Excuse me'. Use 'Is there a...?' to ask about a place. Ask 'How do I get there?' to request directions.
speaking.explanation: This roleplay practises asking for locations and directions in a real-life emergency-like situation. Using 'Is there...?' questions and polite openers is essential for A1 communication in a city.

speaking.instruction: You are at a tourist information centre. Mr. Khoirul works there. Ask him about places to visit in the city. Use 'Are there any...?' questions and describe what kind of places you want to see.
speaking.audioPrompt: Welcome to the City Tourist Information Centre! I'm Mr. Khoirul. What kind of places would you like to visit today?
speaking.scenarioContext: You have just arrived in a new city and you go to the tourist information centre to learn about interesting places to visit. You want to know about museums, parks, and restaurants in the city centre.
speaking.characterRole: Mr. Khoirul is a helpful tourist information officer. He has maps and brochures and loves to recommend places to visitors. He answers questions clearly and gives simple directions.
speaking.targetSentence: Are there any museums in the city centre? I also want to visit a park. Is there a good restaurant near the museum?
speaking.phonetic: /ɑːr ðɛr ˈɛn.i mjuːˈziː.əmz ɪn ðə ˈsɪt.i ˈsɛn.tər? aɪ ˈɔːl.səʊ wɒnt tə ˈvɪz.ɪt ə pɑːk. ɪz ðɛr ə ɡʊd ˈrɛs.tə.rɒnt nɪər ðə mjuːˈziː.əm/
speaking.hint: Use 'Are there any...?' for plural questions and 'Is there a...?' for singular questions. Say what you want to do: 'I want to visit...'
speaking.explanation: This roleplay builds confidence in asking about multiple places using both singular and plural forms of 'there is/are'. Interacting at a tourist centre is a very common A1 real-world scenario.

speaking.instruction: You are helping Mr. Khoirul, a new visitor, find his way around your town. He calls you on the phone and asks for directions from the train station to the library. Give him clear step-by-step directions.
speaking.audioPrompt: Hello! This is Mr. Khoirul. I just arrived at the train station and I need to go to the library. Can you help me? How do I get there?
speaking.scenarioContext: Mr. Khoirul is visiting your town for the first time. He is at the train station and needs to walk to the library. You know the town very well and you need to give him clear, simple directions using imperative verbs and prepositions of place.
speaking.characterRole: Mr. Khoirul is a polite visitor who does not know the town at all. He asks simple questions and needs step-by-step directions. He may ask you to repeat or clarify.
speaking.targetSentence: Go out of the train station and turn right. Go straight down Oak Street. The library is on the left, next to the post office.
speaking.phonetic: /ɡəʊ aʊt ɒv ðə treɪn ˈsteɪ.ʃən ænd tɜːn raɪt. ɡəʊ streɪt daʊn əʊk striːt. ðə ˈlaɪ.brər.i ɪz ɒn ðə lɛft, nɛkst tə ðə pəʊst ˈɒf.ɪs/
speaking.hint: Use imperative verbs to start each direction: 'Go...', 'Turn...', 'Walk...'. Then describe the final location with 'on the left/right' or 'next to'.
speaking.explanation: This roleplay reverses the usual role — you are the direction-giver. Practising giving clear step-by-step directions using imperatives and prepositions is a core A1 speaking skill for real-life navigation.

speaking.instruction: You are at a small shop in the city. Mr. Khoirul is the shopkeeper. Ask him about products in the shop using 'Is there...?' and 'Are there...?' and buy something you need.
speaking.audioPrompt: Good morning! Welcome to my shop. I'm Mr. Khoirul. We have many things here. What are you looking for today?
speaking.scenarioContext: You are shopping in a small city shop. You need to buy a map of the city and some water. You also want to know if the shop sells postcards. Mr. Khoirul is the friendly shopkeeper who can help you find what you need.
speaking.characterRole: Mr. Khoirul is a cheerful shopkeeper in a small city shop. He sells maps, postcards, drinks, snacks, and souvenirs. He is happy to help customers and answers their questions with a smile.
speaking.targetSentence: Good morning! Is there a city map? I need one, please. Are there any postcards? And I would like a bottle of water, please.
speaking.phonetic: /ɡʊd ˈmɔː.nɪŋ! ɪz ðɛr ə ˈsɪt.i mæp? aɪ niːd wʌn pliːz. ɑːr ðɛr ˈɛn.i ˈpəʊst.kɑːdz? ænd aɪ wʊd laɪk ə ˈbɒt.əl ɒv ˈwɔː.tər pliːz/
speaking.hint: Use 'Is there a...?' for one item and 'Are there any...?' for items that might be plural. Always say 'please' to be polite when buying things.
speaking.explanation: This roleplay practises using 'there is/are' in a shopping context, which is a practical A1 skill. Combining location language with transactional language prepares you for real interactions in shops.

speaking.instruction: Say the following sentence out loud. Focus on pronouncing each place name clearly and correctly.
speaking.audioPrompt: Please say this sentence clearly. Pay attention to the place vocabulary words.
speaking.targetSentence: There is a pharmacy between the supermarket and the library.
speaking.phonetic: /ðɛr ɪz ə ˈfɑː.mə.si bɪˈtwiːn ðə ˈsuː.pə.mɑː.kɪt ænd ðə ˈlaɪ.brər.i/
speaking.hint: Say 'PHAR-ma-cy' with stress on the first syllable. 'SU-per-mar-ket' also has stress on the first syllable. 'LI-bra-ry' has stress on the first syllable — do not skip the middle syllable 'bra'.
speaking.explanation: This drill tests your ability to clearly pronounce key city place vocabulary. At A1 level, being able to say place names correctly is essential for asking and giving directions in a town.

speaking.instruction: Say the following sentence out loud. Focus on using the correct form: 'there is' for singular and 'there are' for plural.
speaking.audioPrompt: Please say this sentence. Be careful with 'there is' and 'there are' — one is for singular, the other is for plural.
speaking.targetSentence: There is one hospital in my town, but there are three schools and two parks.
speaking.phonetic: /ðɛr ɪz wʌn ˈhɒs.pɪ.təl ɪn maɪ taʊn, bʌt ðɛr ɑːr θriː skuːlz ænd tuː pɑːks/
speaking.hint: Use 'there IS' before 'one hospital' (singular). Use 'there ARE' before 'three schools' and 'two parks' (plural). Link 'there is' and 'there are' smoothly without long pauses.
speaking.explanation: This grammar drill reinforces the singular/plural distinction between 'there is' and 'there are'. Correct subject-verb agreement in existential sentences is a fundamental A1 grammar point that directly affects how natural your spoken English sounds.

speaking.instruction: Say both words out loud and notice how the syllable stress shifts. First say 'OPPOSITE', then say 'OPPOSITION'. Exaggerate the stressed syllable.
speaking.audioPrompt: Listen carefully to the stress change. Say 'OPPOSITE' — stress on 'OP'. Now say 'OPPOSITION' — stress on 'SI'. Say both words clearly.
speaking.targetSentence: The bank is OPPOSITE the park. There is strong OPPOSITION to the new road.
speaking.phonetic: /ðə bæŋk ɪz ˈɒp.ə.zɪt ðə pɑːk. ðɛr ɪz strɒŋ ˌɒp.əˈzɪʃ.ən tə ðə njuː rəʊd/
speaking.hint: In 'OPPOSITE', stress the first syllable: 'OP-po-site'. In 'OPPOSITION', the stress moves to the third syllable: 'op-po-SI-tion'. Clap on the stressed syllable to feel the rhythm change.
speaking.explanation: This drill practises syllable stress shift between related words. Understanding how stress moves when word forms change is important for clear pronunciation. At A1 level, 'opposite' is a key preposition for describing locations, so pronouncing it correctly is especially useful.

speaking.instruction: Say both sentences out loud. Use RISING intonation (voice goes up) for the yes/no question and FALLING intonation (voice goes down) for the statement. Feel the difference in your voice.
speaking.audioPrompt: Now practise intonation! For the question 'Is there a bank near here?', your voice goes UP at the end. For the statement 'There is a bank on Main Street', your voice goes DOWN at the end. Say both sentences now.
speaking.targetSentence: Is there a bank near here? ↗ There is a bank on Main Street. ↘
speaking.phonetic: /ɪz ðɛr ə bæŋk nɪər hɪər ↗ / /ðɛr ɪz ə bæŋk ɒn meɪn striːt ↘/
speaking.hint: For the question, imagine your voice is climbing stairs at the end — it goes UP on 'here?'. For the statement, imagine your voice is going down a slide — it goes DOWN on 'Street.' Practise the contrast several times.
speaking.explanation: This intonation drill practises the essential difference between rising intonation in yes/no questions and falling intonation in declarative statements. Mastering this pattern helps listeners understand whether you are asking a question or making a statement, which is critical for clear A1-level communication about places and directions.

questions.question: According to the passage, what is in the centre of Greenfield?

There are some shops on Park Road.
There aren't any shops in Greenfield.
questions.answer: There are some shops on Main Street.
questions.explanation: The passage says: 'There are some shops on Main Street.' Notice the use of 'some' in a positive sentence with the plural noun 'shops'.

questions.question: Where is the museum?

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence about restaurants in Greenfield:
questions.explanation: In negative sentences with plural nouns, we use 'there aren't any' — not 'some'. The passage says: 'There aren't any big restaurants here.' This is the correct pattern.

questions.question: What does 'Don't turn right' mean in the passage?
options: It is a warning — do not go right because that road goes to the river.
It is a suggestion to turn right to find the school.
It means you must always turn right.
questions.answer: It is a warning — do not go right because that road goes to the river.
questions.explanation: 'Don't turn right' is a negative imperative. It tells you NOT to do something. Emma explains that turning right takes you to the river, not to the school.

questions.question: Where is the café that Emma likes?
options: In the square, in front of the museum
On Main Street, next to the supermarket
questions.answer: In the square, in front of the museum
questions.explanation: Emma writes: 'I like the café in the square. It is in front of the museum.' The preposition 'in front of' tells us the café faces the museum.

questions.question: Fill in the blank with the correct words: '_______ a small lake in the park.'
questions.explanation: 'Lake' is a singular noun, so we use 'There is'. The passage says: 'There are some beautiful trees and a small lake.' The lake is one item, so 'there is' is correct when we talk about it alone.

questions.question: Emma's school is next to which place?

questions.question: Which plural form is correct?

questions.question: What is the weather like when it is raining?

questions.question: Choose the correct form: 'They _____ playing football right now.'

questions.question: What is Jamie's nationality?

questions.question: Where do they usually eat dinner on weekdays?

questions.instruction: Tell a short story about your town. Describe the places in your town and where they are located. Use 'there is' and 'there are' and prepositions of place. Follow the three story points below to guide your story.
questions.audioPrompt: Now it's your turn to tell me about your town! Describe the places you can find there. Where are they? What is near what? Tell me a short story using 'there is' and 'there are'.
storyPoints: Start by saying the name of your town and mention two or three important places (for example: a school, a hospital, a park).
Describe where these places are using prepositions like 'next to', 'opposite', 'between', or 'behind'.
End by saying what your favourite place is and why you like it (for example: 'My favourite place is the park because it is big and beautiful').
questions.targetSentence: I live in a small town. There is a school next to the hospital. There are two parks near my house. My favourite place is the park because it is big and beautiful.
questions.phonetic: /aɪ lɪv ɪn ə smɔːl taʊn. ðɛr ɪz ə skuːl nɛkst tə ðə ˈhɒs.pɪ.təl. ðɛr ɑːr tuː pɑːks nɪər maɪ haʊs. maɪ ˈfeɪ.vər.ɪt pleɪs ɪz ðə pɑːk bɪˈkɒz ɪt ɪz bɪɡ ænd ˈbjuː.tɪ.fəl/
questions.hint: Remember to use 'there is' for one thing and 'there are' for two or more things. Use prepositions like 'next to', 'near', 'opposite' to describe locations.
questions.explanation: This storytelling task helps you practise describing places in your town using existential structures ('there is/are') and prepositions of place. Speaking in connected sentences builds your fluency and confidence at A1 level.

questions.instruction: Tell a short story about walking through a city centre. Describe what you see and the directions you take. Use imperative verbs like 'turn', 'go', and 'cross', and describe places using 'there is' and 'there are'.
questions.audioPrompt: Imagine you are walking through a city centre. Tell me what you see and how you walk from one place to another. Use direction words and describe the places around you!
storyPoints: Start at a specific place (for example: 'I start at the train station') and describe what is near it.
Give directions to walk to another place (for example: 'I turn left and go straight. There is a big supermarket on the right').
Arrive at your final destination and describe what is around it (for example: 'I arrive at the museum. There are beautiful gardens opposite the museum').
questions.targetSentence: I start at the train station. There is a café next to the station. I turn left and go straight down Main Street. There is a big supermarket on the right. I cross the road and arrive at the museum. There are beautiful gardens opposite the museum.
questions.phonetic: /aɪ stɑːt æt ðə treɪn ˈsteɪ.ʃən. ðɛr ɪz ə ˈkæf.eɪ nɛkst tə ðə ˈsteɪ.ʃən. aɪ tɜːn lɛft ænd ɡəʊ streɪt daʊn meɪn striːt. ðɛr ɪz ə bɪɡ ˈsuː.pə.mɑː.kɪt ɒn ðə raɪt. aɪ krɒs ðə rəʊd ænd əˈraɪv æt ðə mjuːˈziː.əm. ðɛr ɑːr ˈbjuː.tɪ.fəl ˈɡɑː.dənz ˈɒp.ə.zɪt ðə mjuːˈziː.əm/
questions.hint: Use imperative verbs at the start of direction sentences: 'Turn left', 'Go straight', 'Cross the road'. Then describe what you see with 'there is' or 'there are'.
questions.explanation: This storytelling task combines direction-giving with place descriptions. Practising both skills together helps you speak more naturally when navigating or describing a city, which is a key real-world A1 speaking skill.

questions.instruction: You are a tourist in a new city. You are lost and you call Mr. Khoirul, a local guide, to ask for directions to the nearest hospital. Use polite questions with 'Is there...?' and listen to his directions.
questions.audioPrompt: Ring ring! Hello, this is Mr. Khoirul, your local city guide. How can I help you today?
questions.scenarioContext: You are a tourist visiting a new city for the first time. You feel unwell and need to find the nearest hospital. You call Mr. Khoirul, a friendly local guide, to ask where the hospital is and how to get there from the main square.
questions.characterRole: Mr. Khoirul is a friendly and patient local city guide who knows every street and building in the city. He speaks slowly and clearly to help tourists find their way.
questions.targetSentence: Excuse me, is there a hospital near here? How do I get there from the main square?
questions.phonetic: /ɪkˈskjuːz miː, ɪz ðɛr ə ˈhɒs.pɪ.təl nɪər hɪər? haʊ duː aɪ ɡɛt ðɛr frɒm ðə meɪn skwɛər/
questions.hint: Start politely with 'Excuse me'. Use 'Is there a...?' to ask about a place. Ask 'How do I get there?' to request directions.
questions.explanation: This roleplay practises asking for locations and directions in a real-life emergency-like situation. Using 'Is there...?' questions and polite openers is essential for A1 communication in a city.

questions.instruction: You are at a tourist information centre. Mr. Khoirul works there. Ask him about places to visit in the city. Use 'Are there any...?' questions and describe what kind of places you want to see.
questions.audioPrompt: Welcome to the City Tourist Information Centre! I'm Mr. Khoirul. What kind of places would you like to visit today?
questions.scenarioContext: You have just arrived in a new city and you go to the tourist information centre to learn about interesting places to visit. You want to know about museums, parks, and restaurants in the city centre.
questions.characterRole: Mr. Khoirul is a helpful tourist information officer. He has maps and brochures and loves to recommend places to visitors. He answers questions clearly and gives simple directions.
questions.targetSentence: Are there any museums in the city centre? I also want to visit a park. Is there a good restaurant near the museum?
questions.phonetic: /ɑːr ðɛr ˈɛn.i mjuːˈziː.əmz ɪn ðə ˈsɪt.i ˈsɛn.tər? aɪ ˈɔːl.səʊ wɒnt tə ˈvɪz.ɪt ə pɑːk. ɪz ðɛr ə ɡʊd ˈrɛs.tə.rɒnt nɪər ðə mjuːˈziː.əm/
questions.hint: Use 'Are there any...?' for plural questions and 'Is there a...?' for singular questions. Say what you want to do: 'I want to visit...'
questions.explanation: This roleplay builds confidence in asking about multiple places using both singular and plural forms of 'there is/are'. Interacting at a tourist centre is a very common A1 real-world scenario.

questions.instruction: You are helping Mr. Khoirul, a new visitor, find his way around your town. He calls you on the phone and asks for directions from the train station to the library. Give him clear step-by-step directions.
questions.audioPrompt: Hello! This is Mr. Khoirul. I just arrived at the train station and I need to go to the library. Can you help me? How do I get there?
questions.scenarioContext: Mr. Khoirul is visiting your town for the first time. He is at the train station and needs to walk to the library. You know the town very well and you need to give him clear, simple directions using imperative verbs and prepositions of place.
questions.characterRole: Mr. Khoirul is a polite visitor who does not know the town at all. He asks simple questions and needs step-by-step directions. He may ask you to repeat or clarify.
questions.targetSentence: Go out of the train station and turn right. Go straight down Oak Street. The library is on the left, next to the post office.
questions.phonetic: /ɡəʊ aʊt ɒv ðə treɪn ˈsteɪ.ʃən ænd tɜːn raɪt. ɡəʊ streɪt daʊn əʊk striːt. ðə ˈlaɪ.brər.i ɪz ɒn ðə lɛft, nɛkst tə ðə pəʊst ˈɒf.ɪs/
questions.hint: Use imperative verbs to start each direction: 'Go...', 'Turn...', 'Walk...'. Then describe the final location with 'on the left/right' or 'next to'.
questions.explanation: This roleplay reverses the usual role — you are the direction-giver. Practising giving clear step-by-step directions using imperatives and prepositions is a core A1 speaking skill for real-life navigation.

questions.instruction: You are at a small shop in the city. Mr. Khoirul is the shopkeeper. Ask him about products in the shop using 'Is there...?' and 'Are there...?' and buy something you need.
questions.audioPrompt: Good morning! Welcome to my shop. I'm Mr. Khoirul. We have many things here. What are you looking for today?
questions.scenarioContext: You are shopping in a small city shop. You need to buy a map of the city and some water. You also want to know if the shop sells postcards. Mr. Khoirul is the friendly shopkeeper who can help you find what you need.
questions.characterRole: Mr. Khoirul is a cheerful shopkeeper in a small city shop. He sells maps, postcards, drinks, snacks, and souvenirs. He is happy to help customers and answers their questions with a smile.
questions.targetSentence: Good morning! Is there a city map? I need one, please. Are there any postcards? And I would like a bottle of water, please.
questions.phonetic: /ɡʊd ˈmɔː.nɪŋ! ɪz ðɛr ə ˈsɪt.i mæp? aɪ niːd wʌn pliːz. ɑːr ðɛr ˈɛn.i ˈpəʊst.kɑːdz? ænd aɪ wʊd laɪk ə ˈbɒt.əl ɒv ˈwɔː.tər pliːz/
questions.hint: Use 'Is there a...?' for one item and 'Are there any...?' for items that might be plural. Always say 'please' to be polite when buying things.
questions.explanation: This roleplay practises using 'there is/are' in a shopping context, which is a practical A1 skill. Combining location language with transactional language prepares you for real interactions in shops.

questions.instruction: Say the following sentence out loud. Focus on pronouncing each place name clearly and correctly.
questions.audioPrompt: Please say this sentence clearly. Pay attention to the place vocabulary words.
questions.targetSentence: There is a pharmacy between the supermarket and the library.
questions.phonetic: /ðɛr ɪz ə ˈfɑː.mə.si bɪˈtwiːn ðə ˈsuː.pə.mɑː.kɪt ænd ðə ˈlaɪ.brər.i/
questions.hint: Say 'PHAR-ma-cy' with stress on the first syllable. 'SU-per-mar-ket' also has stress on the first syllable. 'LI-bra-ry' has stress on the first syllable — do not skip the middle syllable 'bra'.
questions.explanation: This drill tests your ability to clearly pronounce key city place vocabulary. At A1 level, being able to say place names correctly is essential for asking and giving directions in a town.

questions.instruction: Say the following sentence out loud. Focus on using the correct form: 'there is' for singular and 'there are' for plural.
questions.audioPrompt: Please say this sentence. Be careful with 'there is' and 'there are' — one is for singular, the other is for plural.
questions.targetSentence: There is one hospital in my town, but there are three schools and two parks.
questions.phonetic: /ðɛr ɪz wʌn ˈhɒs.pɪ.təl ɪn maɪ taʊn, bʌt ðɛr ɑːr θriː skuːlz ænd tuː pɑːks/
questions.hint: Use 'there IS' before 'one hospital' (singular). Use 'there ARE' before 'three schools' and 'two parks' (plural). Link 'there is' and 'there are' smoothly without long pauses.
questions.explanation: This grammar drill reinforces the singular/plural distinction between 'there is' and 'there are'. Correct subject-verb agreement in existential sentences is a fundamental A1 grammar point that directly affects how natural your spoken English sounds.

questions.instruction: Say both words out loud and notice how the syllable stress shifts. First say 'OPPOSITE', then say 'OPPOSITION'. Exaggerate the stressed syllable.
questions.audioPrompt: Listen carefully to the stress change. Say 'OPPOSITE' — stress on 'OP'. Now say 'OPPOSITION' — stress on 'SI'. Say both words clearly.
questions.targetSentence: The bank is OPPOSITE the park. There is strong OPPOSITION to the new road.
questions.phonetic: /ðə bæŋk ɪz ˈɒp.ə.zɪt ðə pɑːk. ðɛr ɪz strɒŋ ˌɒp.əˈzɪʃ.ən tə ðə njuː rəʊd/
questions.hint: In 'OPPOSITE', stress the first syllable: 'OP-po-site'. In 'OPPOSITION', the stress moves to the third syllable: 'op-po-SI-tion'. Clap on the stressed syllable to feel the rhythm change.
questions.explanation: This drill practises syllable stress shift between related words. Understanding how stress moves when word forms change is important for clear pronunciation. At A1 level, 'opposite' is a key preposition for describing locations, so pronouncing it correctly is especially useful.

questions.instruction: Say both sentences out loud. Use RISING intonation (voice goes up) for the yes/no question and FALLING intonation (voice goes down) for the statement. Feel the difference in your voice.
questions.audioPrompt: Now practise intonation! For the question 'Is there a bank near here?', your voice goes UP at the end. For the statement 'There is a bank on Main Street', your voice goes DOWN at the end. Say both sentences now.
questions.targetSentence: Is there a bank near here? ↗ There is a bank on Main Street. ↘
questions.phonetic: /ɪz ðɛr ə bæŋk nɪər hɪər ↗ / /ðɛr ɪz ə bæŋk ɒn meɪn striːt ↘/
questions.hint: For the question, imagine your voice is climbing stairs at the end — it goes UP on 'here?'. For the statement, imagine your voice is going down a slide — it goes DOWN on 'Street.' Practise the contrast several times.
questions.explanation: This intonation drill practises the essential difference between rising intonation in yes/no questions and falling intonation in declarative statements. Mastering this pattern helps listeners understand whether you are asking a question or making a statement, which is critical for clear A1-level communication about places and directions.

practicumQuestions.question: Choose the correct sentence about restaurants in Greenfield:
practicumQuestions.explanation: In negative sentences with plural nouns, we use 'there aren't any' — not 'some'. The passage says: 'There aren't any big restaurants here.' This is the correct pattern.

practicumQuestions.question: What does 'Don't turn right' mean in the passage?

On Main Street, next to the supermarket

practicumQuestions.question: Emma's school is next to which place?

practicumQuestions.explanation: Bentuk jamak dari 'this child is' adalah 'these children are'.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Bandingkan dua hal ini menggunakan kata sifat 'tall':
practicumQuestions.hint: Gunakan 'taller than'.
targetAnswers: Alex is taller than Leo.
Alex is taller than Leo
practicumQuestions.explanation: Comparative untuk kata sifat satu suku kata menambahkan akhiran -er: taller than.
